question: why doesn't the personal os just keep all my data in its own database?

must: Each service stays the source of truth for what it owns (Obsidian for notes, Google for calendar and tasks, etc.)
The Personal OS is a layer on top (unified search, navigation, capture, dashboard) and keeps only app state, mappings and indexes locally
also: External systems should not be duplicated unnecessarily

question: why obsidian and not notion for storing notes?

must: Markdown files on disk are the least lock-in-prone format, so the knowledge survives if the project is abandoned
No API, OAuth or rate limits, so the first integration focuses on the genuinely hard parts
also: Notion would add API auth on day one, and its block model is heavier to parse

question: why did we skip an ORM, wouldn't it make switching databases easier?

must: The SQL that matters here (full-text search, GIN indexes, ranking, later pgvector) is exactly what an ORM hides, and writing it is the point
Easier switching is irrelevant because Postgres is a deliberate choice, not a detail to abstract away
also: The schema is small, so Alembic's team-migration value does not apply

question: why do we write the Google and GitHub connections ourselves instead of using existing MCP servers?

must: For backend integrations, MCP adds a process and an extra auth hop for no gain; direct APIs are simpler (one OAuth client covers the Google services)
also: MCP is for giving tools to an AI model; the Personal OS uses it to expose itself
Hand-written providers give control over errors, pagination and rate limits, with no dependence on community servers

question: what protections did I have to build before the app was allowed to change files in my vault?

must: Atomic writes: write to a temp file, then rename, never overwriting in place
A snapshot of the previous version before any change
An undo path that restores the snapshot
Tests covering partial-write and permission failures
Confirmation before modifying a file
also: Undo refuses if the note was edited after routing
Filenames are sanitised

question: why not just use the file name to identify a note everywhere in the app?

must: File paths change when notes are renamed, so everything refers to a stable internal id (entity_map) instead
also: Identity is the hardest thing to retrofit later
Stable ids connect the same thing across services

question: why is the AI tracing tool planned to run on my own machine instead of a hosted service?

must: Traces contain text from the notes, so a hosted service would mean vault content leaving the machine
also: It is decided but not built yet

question: how do we decide when to use a ready-made library versus writing it ourselves?

must: Adopt the tool when it provides weeks of engineering
Build it yourself when the requirements are known and the code is short
When the code is short but the design space is unknown, read the mature tool first, then write a small version (catalogue, then build)
also: Adopt only if the simpler version can be sketched first
Record an exit trigger for every adoption

question: why doesn't the AI part just copy all my notes into the database so searching is faster?

must: Ingestion means indexing, not owning: it creates derived data (index entries, embeddings), never a canonical copy, and Obsidian stays the source of truth
also: Deleting all ingested data must only cost a reindex; a full copy would become a second source of truth that goes stale

question: why did we choose RabbitMQ for the background job queue?
why not use a simple single-file database for an app only I use?

must: Postgres full-text search is meaningfully better than SQLite's for unified search
pgvector is one extension away, avoiding a database migration when embeddings arrive
also: SQLite was defensible and simpler; the trade-off was made deliberately

question: why not use one of the popular AI frameworks to wire up the retrieval pipeline?

must: The parts a framework would replace already exist or are short to build, so it adds a dependency without adding capability
It would hide what the project needs to see and control (the SQL, the request shape); LlamaIndex also assumes it owns the documents, conflicting with Obsidian as the source of truth
also: LangGraph is deferred, not rejected

question: which cloud provider are we going to host this on?

must: None, deliberately: AWS and GCP are skipped because the tool reads a local vault, and deploying would mean syncing it to the cloud (breaking ADR-001) or connecting back home
also: Revisit if the Personal OS is wanted on a phone

also: Simple boilerplate may be built directly but must be explained afterwards
